title: A3 — High-performing storage
bodyMarkdown:
## High-performing storage

Exam task **3.1**. Lessons 2.1 and 2.2 already covered EBS, EFS, and S3 basics, durability, and cost. This lesson focuses on **performance and scalability**: which configuration to pick when a requirement names throughput, IOPS, latency, request rate, or future growth.

### K01 — Hybrid storage solutions to meet business requirements

**AWS Storage Gateway** connects on-premises applications to AWS storage without a rewrite. It offers three current gateway types. **Amazon S3 File Gateway** presents an NFS or SMB file share backed by an S3 bucket, with a local cache for low-latency access to recently used files. **Volume Gateway** presents block volumes over iSCSI in two modes: **cached volumes** keep primary data in Amazon S3 and cache the working set locally, so on-premises storage stays small; **stored volumes** keep the full dataset on-premises for low-latency local access and asynchronously back up point-in-time snapshots to Amazon S3. **Tape Gateway** presents a virtual tape library to existing backup software, storing virtual tapes in S3 and, for long-term archival, in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive. **Amazon FSx File Gateway** (for on-premises access to FSx for Windows File Server) is no longer available to new customers, so pick S3 File Gateway or a direct FSx for Windows File Server connection over a VPN or Direct Connect link instead.

For moving data into AWS rather than keeping some of it on-premises indefinitely, compare **AWS DataSync** with the discontinued Snow Family devices. DataSync is an online transfer service: an agent reads from an on-premises NFS share, SMB share, HDFS cluster, or self-managed object store and writes into Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, or Amazon FSx (Windows File Server, Lustre, OpenZFS, or ONTAP), preserving permissions and metadata, with built-in encryption, integrity checks, and a purpose-built protocol that can saturate a 10 Gbps link from a single task. **AWS Snowball Edge is no longer available to new customers** — AWS now points new customers to DataSync for online transfers and to **AWS Data Transfer Terminal**, a physical facility with high-speed fiber connections, for large offline transfers instead of shipping an appliance.

**Exam tip:** a scenario needing a persistent NFS/SMB share backed by S3 is an S3 File Gateway; iSCSI block volumes with an on-premises cache point to Volume Gateway; a scenario built around shipping a physical appliance describes the retired Snow Family model — the current answer for a slow or unreliable link is DataSync (online) or Data Transfer Terminal (offline).

### K02 — Storage services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon EBS)

Beyond the S3/EFS/EBS basics from lesson 2.2, the **FSx** family adds purpose-built file systems for specific performance needs. **Amazon FSx for Lustre** is built for high-performance computing and machine learning: it delivers hundreds of gigabytes per second of throughput and millions of IOPS across thousands of concurrently mounted EC2 instances, and it can link directly to an S3 bucket so objects are readable as files without a separate copy step. Choose **Scratch** deployment for short-lived, non-replicated processing where losing data on a server failure is acceptable, and **Persistent** deployment when the file system must outlive any single compute job. **Amazon FSx for Windows File Server** provides a fully managed native Windows file system over SMB, with Active Directory integration, for Windows-based applications that need real NTFS semantics. **Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP** brings NetApp's ONTAP engine to AWS with multi-protocol access (NFS, SMB, and iSCSI on the same volume), snapshots, and storage efficiency features such as deduplication and compression, fitting an existing NetApp shop moving to AWS. **Amazon FSx for OpenZFS** exposes ZFS features (snapshots, cloning, compression) over NFS, with an in-memory read cache that can push a single file system past 1,000,000 IOPS at sub-millisecond latency.

**Exam tip:** "thousands of compute nodes, HPC or ML training data, tied to an S3 data lake" is FSx for Lustre; "lift-and-shift a Windows file server with Active Directory" is FSx for Windows File Server; "existing NetApp snapshots and multi-protocol access" is FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

### K03 — Storage types with associated characteristics (for example, object, file, block)

**Block storage (Amazon EBS)** comes in five volume types with different performance profiles. **gp3** is the default general-purpose SSD: it delivers a baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s throughput at no extra cost, and each can be provisioned independently of size up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s, with performance sustained indefinitely (no bursting). **gp2** is the older general-purpose SSD whose IOPS scale with volume size (3 IOPS/GiB baseline) and uses a burst-credit model instead — gp3 is preferred for new volumes because performance and size are decoupled. **io2 Block Express** is the highest-performance EBS type: up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s on Nitro-based instances, sub-millisecond average latency, and 99.999% durability, for the most demanding mission-critical databases. The two HDD types price by throughput, not IOPS, and neither supports being a boot volume: **st1** (Throughput Optimized HDD) fits large sequential workloads accessed frequently (log processing, big-data, streaming), with baseline throughput of 40 MiB/s per TiB, burst throughput of 250 MiB/s per TiB, and a per-volume cap of 500 MiB/s; **sc1** (Cold HDD) is the cheapest option for infrequently accessed sequential data, with a lower baseline of 12 MiB/s per TiB, burst of 80 MiB/s per TiB, and a 250 MiB/s cap. **Instance store** volumes are physically attached NVMe or SSD disks on the host: they deliver very high, low-latency local IOPS but the data is lost when the instance stops, hibernates, terminates, or the underlying disk fails — use them only for caches, buffers, or data replicated elsewhere, never as the only copy.

**File storage (Amazon EFS)** performance depends on two independent settings. **Performance mode** is fixed at creation: **General Purpose** has the lowest per-operation latency and is the recommended default; **Max I/O** trades higher per-operation latency for higher aggregate throughput and IOPS across a very large number of concurrently connected clients, and should only be chosen when General Purpose measurably bottlenecks. **Throughput mode** can be changed later: **Bursting** throughput scales with the amount of data stored and uses a credit-based burst bucket, so a small file system can throttle under sustained load; **Provisioned** throughput lets you set a fixed MiB/s independent of storage size, for a small, hot file system; **Elastic** throughput (the default for new file systems) scales automatically up and down with your workload's demand, with no capacity planning at all, and Regional file systems using Elastic throughput can drive up to 1,500 MiBps of combined read/write with a current client. EFS also offers Standard and One Zone storage classes, plus Infrequent Access tiers within each, trading a single Availability Zone (lower cost, lower resilience) against Standard's multi-AZ redundancy.

**Object storage (Amazon S3)** now includes **S3 Express One Zone**, a storage class for directory buckets that trades multi-AZ redundancy for consistent single-digit-millisecond first-byte latency — up to 10 times faster than S3 Standard — by co-locating storage with compute in one Availability Zone. A directory bucket defaults to 200,000 reads and 100,000 writes per second, and can scale to 2,000,000 reads and 200,000 writes per second, well beyond a general purpose bucket's per-prefix guidance.

**Exam tip:** "many EC2 instances, highest possible aggregate throughput across a huge fleet of clients" is EFS Max I/O; "smallest, most latency-sensitive workload, single AZ acceptable" is S3 Express One Zone; "sub-millisecond latency, mission-critical database" is io2 Block Express, not gp3.

### S01 — Determining storage services and configurations that meet performance demands

Match the requirement's specific performance language to the right lever, not just the right service. For **S3**, a single object's GET or PUT throughput is improved with **byte-range fetches** — concurrent `Range` GET requests against the same object, typically in 8–16 MB chunks, to parallelize a large download and improve retry behavior — and a large object's upload throughput improves with **multipart upload**, which splits the object into parts uploaded in parallel and reassembled by S3. When the client is geographically far from the bucket's Region, **S3 Transfer Acceleration** routes the upload through the nearest CloudFront edge location and over AWS's backbone network instead of the public internet, cutting the distance-driven latency. For a workload issuing a very high number of requests, spread the load across **multiple key prefixes**: S3 scales request rate per prefix and has no limit on the number of prefixes in a bucket, so more prefixes means more aggregate throughput, and S3 also scales automatically to absorb a gradual increase in request rate.

For **block** and **file** performance requirements, translate the number in the stem directly into a volume type or EFS setting: a database needing guaranteed low double-digit-thousand IOPS with the lowest possible latency needs io2 Block Express, not gp3; a large sequential ETL job needs st1's throughput profile, not an SSD; a fleet of render or analytics nodes hammering one file system with many small, parallel operations needs EFS Max I/O with Elastic throughput, not General Purpose with Provisioned throughput; and a single-node HPC job reading a huge dataset repeatedly needs FSx for Lustre, not EFS.

**Exam tip:** when a stem gives you a number (IOPS, MiB/s, milliseconds, requests per second), it is telling you exactly which volume type, throughput mode, or S3 technique to pick — match the number to the service's documented ceiling rather than guessing from the service name alone.

### S02 — Determining storage services that can scale to accommodate future needs

Favor services that scale without a forklift upgrade. **Amazon S3** has effectively unlimited object storage capacity with no capacity to plan ahead of time — you never provision size. **Amazon EBS** volumes scale using **Elastic Volumes**: you can increase size, change volume type (for example gp3 to io2 Block Express), or raise provisioned IOPS and throughput while the volume stays attached and in use, with no downtime — but a volume still lives in one Availability Zone and tops out at 64 TiB, so a workload that will outgrow a single volume needs to plan for striping across volumes or a different service from the start. **Amazon EFS** grows and shrinks automatically as files are added and removed — there is no size to provision — and with **Elastic throughput mode**, available bandwidth scales automatically with demand, so a file system built for today's load does not need to be resized as usage grows. **FSx for Lustre, ONTAP, and OpenZFS** all support increasing storage capacity and, on most deployment types, throughput capacity after creation, without recreating the file system. For migration workloads that must grow with the data volume, **DataSync** scales by running more tasks in parallel or adding agents, rather than by ordering a bigger physical device — a path that no longer exists now that Snowball Edge is closed to new customers.

**Exam tip:** "must grow without a resize project later" favors S3 or EFS, which need no capacity planning at all; "must grow but stays on a single volume" favors EBS Elastic Volumes, planned with headroom under the 64 TiB ceiling.

### Warnings

- Do not use the AWS root user for routine lab work.
- Stopping an instance is not teardown.
- $10 budget alerts warn; they do not stop spend.
